questions.question: The chapter's opening sentence frames the whole book around a distinction. Which is it, and what does it say is rarely the limiting factor?

options.text: Stateless vs stateful applications; network bandwidth is rarely limiting
Data-intensive vs compute-intensive applications; raw CPU power is rarely limiting
OLTP vs OLAP applications; disk capacity is rarely limiting
Monolithic vs distributed applications; memory is rarely limiting

questions.explanation: Many applications today are data-intensive, as opposed to compute-intensive. Raw CPU power is rarely a limiting factor for them.

questions.question: For data-intensive applications, which three things does the chapter name as the bigger problems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The amount of data
The complexity of data
The cost of CPU cycles
The speed at which the data is changing

questions.explanation: Amount, complexity, and speed of change. Three separate growth axes — the scalability section's insistence on naming which dimension grows begins here.

questions.question: Which standard building block does the chapter attach to the need 'remember the result of an expensive operation, to speed up reads'?

options.text: Search indexes
Batch processing
Caches
Stream processing

questions.explanation: Caches. Note the precise wording: the need is about speeding up reads by remembering an expensive result, not about storage.

questions.question: The chapter's stated need for a database is to store data so that ______ can find it again later.

options.text: you
they, or another application,
the operations team
any authorized user

questions.explanation: 'Store data so that they, or another application, can find it again later.' Persistence is for other programs too, not just for you.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say the list of building blocks may sound 'painfully obvious'?

options.text: Because these data systems are such a successful abstraction that we use them without thinking too much
Because the list is incomplete and simplified for beginners
Because most engineers have already built each one from scratch
Because vendors market them so heavily

questions.explanation: A good abstraction's payoff is that it stops being visible as a choice: 'most engineers wouldn't dream of writing a new data storage engine from scratch, because databases are a perfectly good tool for the job.'

questions.question: Having called the building blocks a successful abstraction, the chapter immediately raises two difficulties. Which two? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Choice — many systems with different characteristics, because different applications have different requirements
Combination — it can be hard to combine tools when one tool cannot do the job alone
Cost — licensing fees dominate the budget
Staffing — few engineers understand storage engines

questions.explanation: Choice and combination. The second drives what follows: combining tools is what produces a composite, special-purpose data system.

questions.question: A database and a message queue both store data for some time, yet the chapter calls them very different categories. Which two reasons does it give for lumping them together as 'data systems' anyway? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The categories have blurred
Applications now need several tools stitched together
They share the same query language
They are sold by the same vendors

questions.explanation: Boundaries between categories have blurred, and applications increasingly need several tools stitched together to meet their requirements.

questions.question: You add a Memcached caching layer and an Elasticsearch server alongside your main database. Whose responsibility is it to keep them in sync?

options.text: The database's replication subsystem
The application code's
The cache's write-through policy
The operations team's monitoring

questions.explanation: The application code's. And that is the moment the chapter says you are now a data system designer.

questions.question: Once you combine several tools behind one API, what does the chapter say follows?

options.text: You can stop reasoning about the individual tools
Your composite service now makes guarantees of its own, and you are not only an application developer but also a data system designer
The weakest tool's guarantees automatically apply to the whole
Performance becomes the sum of the components' performance

questions.explanation: You have created a new, special-purpose data system from smaller, general-purpose components — and it carries guarantees of its own.

questions.question: Match the concern to the chapter's own definition: 'Over time many different people will work on the system, and they should all be able to work on it productively.'

options.text: Reliability
Scalability
Maintainability
Operability

questions.explanation: Maintainability. Note it is defined in terms of people, not code — operability, simplicity and evolvability are its three sub-principles.

questions.question: Which is the chapter's compressed definition of reliability?

options.text: Never failing under any circumstances
Continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong
Recovering quickly after a failure
Meeting the agreed service level agreement

questions.explanation: 'Continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong.' Reliability is not the absence of faults but correctness in their presence.

questions.question: The chapter lists four typical expectations that add up to 'working correctly'. Which one is the odd one out because it is not about correctness at all?

options.text: The application performs the function the user expected
It tolerates the user making mistakes or using the software in unexpected ways
Its performance is good enough under the expected load and data volume
The system prevents any unauthorized access and abuse

questions.explanation: Security. It is easy to forget in a list about correctness, yet the chapter includes it in what 'working correctly' means.

questions.question: Define fault and failure as the chapter does.

options.text: A fault is one component deviating from its spec; a failure is the system as a whole stopping to provide the required service to the user
A fault is a user error; a failure is a hardware error
A fault is recoverable; a failure is permanent
A fault is detected by monitoring; a failure is reported by customers

questions.explanation: The design conclusion: reducing the probability of faults to zero is the wrong target, so you build fault-tolerance mechanisms that prevent faults from causing failures.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call the term 'fault-tolerant' slightly misleading?

options.text: Because tolerance implies the fault was expected
Because it suggests a system could tolerate every possible kind of fault, which is not feasible — it only makes sense to talk about tolerating certain types of faults
Because no system has ever achieved it
Because the term comes from hardware engineering and does not apply to software

questions.explanation: Hence the black-hole remark: tolerating a black hole swallowing Earth would require web hosting in space, so the claim must always be scoped to fault types.

questions.question: Why can it make sense to deliberately increase the rate of faults in a fault-tolerant system?

options.text: To exercise the fault-tolerance machinery so that rarely-used error handling does not silently rot — the approach behind Netflix's Chaos Monkey
To reduce the mean time to failure of individual components
To satisfy audit requirements
To make percentile measurements more representative

questions.explanation: Many high-severity bugs are caused by poor error handling; deliberately triggering faults ensures the tolerance mechanism is continually tested.

questions.question: The chapter generally prefers tolerating faults to preventing them, but names an exception. Which, and what makes it exceptional?

options.text: Hardware faults, because they are uncorrelated
Security, because if an attacker has compromised a system and gained access to sensitive data, that event cannot be undone
Human error, because humans are unreliable
Software bugs, because they are correlated across nodes

questions.explanation: Security matters cannot be undone, so prevention is preferred there.

questions.question: Hard disks are reported to have an MTTF of about 10 to 50 years. On a storage cluster with 10,000 disks, what does the chapter say you should expect?

options.text: One disk to die per week
One disk to die per day
One disk to die per hour
One disk to die per month

questions.explanation: 10,000 disks at a 10-year MTTF gives about 2.7 deaths/day; at 50 years about 0.55/day. The chapter's 'on average one disk to die per day' sits inside that band.

questions.question: Which hardware-redundancy measures does the chapter name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disks in a RAID configuration
Dual power supplies and hot-swappable CPUs
Batteries and diesel generators for backup power
Error-correcting DNS resolvers

questions.explanation: The honest claim attached to them: they cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures, but the approach is well understood and can often keep a machine running uninterrupted for years.

questions.question: Until recently, hardware redundancy alone sufficed for most applications. What exact condition did that argument depend on?

options.text: That the application had fewer than 100 users
That you can restore a backup onto a new machine fairly quickly
That the disks were enterprise-grade
That the datacenter had two independent power feeds

questions.explanation: Single-machine redundancy plus fast restore made full high availability unnecessary for most non-critical applications.

questions.question: Which two trends broke the 'hardware redundancy is enough' assumption? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data volumes and appetites for computing have grown, so applications use larger numbers of machines, raising the rate of hardware faults
Cloud platforms such as AWS are designed for flexibility and elasticity over single-machine reliability, so instances can become unavailable without warning
Disks became fundamentally less reliable than in the 1990s
Operating systems stopped supporting RAID

questions.explanation: The software-fault-tolerance systems that replaced single-machine redundancy also bring an operational benefit: nodes can be patched one at a time, so a rolling upgrade needs no planned downtime.

questions.question: Along which axis does the chapter contrast hardware faults with systematic software errors, and what follows?

options.text: Cost — software errors are cheaper to fix, so they matter less
Correlation — software errors are correlated across nodes and so tend to cause many more system failures than uncorrelated hardware faults
Detectability — software errors are always caught by monitoring
Frequency — hardware faults are far more frequent

questions.explanation: Adding redundant nodes does not help against a bug that is present in every instance.

questions.question: Which systematic software error does the chapter give with a date and cause?

options.text: The leap second on June 30, 2012 that caused many applications to hang simultaneously, due to a bug in the Linux kernel
The Y2K rollover on January 1, 2000 caused by two-digit years
The AWS S3 outage of February 28, 2017 caused by a typo in a runbook command
The Knight Capital trading loss of August 1, 2012 caused by a stale deployment

questions.explanation: The other examples it gives: a runaway process using up a shared resource, a service the system depends on slowing down or returning corrupted responses, and cascading failures.

questions.question: Why do systematic software bugs 'lie dormant for a long time' before firing?

options.text: They require an unusual set of circumstances; until then the software works fine, and what is revealed is that it was making an assumption about its environment that stopped being true
They are introduced only during upgrades
Compilers optimize them away until load increases
They depend on the disk filling up

questions.explanation: The leap-second bug's assumption was that time moves forward monotonically, one second per second.

questions.question: The chapter's first human-error mitigation is 'design systems in a way that minimizes opportunities for error'. Which caveat does it attach immediately?

options.text: That such designs are expensive to build
That if the interfaces are too restrictive people will work around them, negating their benefit — a tricky balance to get right
That it only works for internal tools
That it must be combined with training

questions.explanation: Well-designed abstractions, APIs and admin interfaces make it easy to do the right thing — but over-restriction is self-defeating.

questions.question: The chapter demands two properties of the sandbox where people can explore and experiment. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fully featured, so it exercises the real code paths
Using real data, so the behaviour observed is representative
Isolated on a separate physical network
Reset automatically every hour

questions.explanation: Fully featured and using real data, but without affecting real users — that is what decouples the place mistakes are made from the place they cause failures.

questions.question: Which levels of testing does the chapter list, and what does it say automated testing is especially valuable for?

options.text: Unit tests only; valuable for regression protection
Unit tests to whole-system integration tests and manual tests; automated testing is especially valuable for covering corner cases that rarely arise in normal operation
Integration and load tests; valuable for finding performance regressions
Chaos tests only; valuable for validating fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Manual tests are explicitly in the list — the chapter does not claim everything can be automated.

questions.question: Which three recovery mechanisms does the chapter list for limiting the impact of human error? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fast rollback of configuration changes
Gradual rollout of new code, so unexpected bugs affect only a small subset of users
Tools to recompute data, in case the old computation was incorrect
Mandatory four-eyes review of every change

questions.explanation: Each buys a different kind of reversibility: config, code, and derived data.

questions.question: What does the chapter call monitoring as other engineering disciplines do, and what analogy does it use?

options.text: Instrumentation; the analogy of a car dashboard
Telemetry; once a rocket has left the ground, telemetry is essential for tracking what is happening and for understanding failures
Auditing; the analogy of financial accounting
Observability; the analogy of a medical scan

questions.explanation: Its three distinct jobs: early warning signals, checking whether assumptions or constraints are being violated, and diagnosing after an incident.

questions.question: Which human-error mitigation does the chapter explicitly place beyond its own scope?

options.text: Detailed and clear monitoring
Good management practices and training
Sandbox environments
Quick and easy recovery

questions.explanation: It calls them a complex and important aspect, and beyond the scope of the book.

questions.question: Under what circumstances does the chapter permit consciously sacrificing reliability, and with what condition?

options.text: Never — reliability is always paramount
To reduce development cost (e.g. a prototype for an unproven market) or operational cost (a service with a narrow profit margin) — but we should be very conscious of when we are cutting corners
Only when an SLA explicitly permits it
Only for internal tools with no external users

questions.explanation: Cutting corners is allowed; doing it unknowingly is not.

questions.question: How does the chapter define scalability, and why does it call both 'X is scalable' and 'Y doesn't scale' meaningless?

options.text: A system's ability to cope with increased load; scalability is not a one-dimensional label, so the meaningful discussion is 'if the system grows in a particular way, what are our options for coping with the growth?'
The maximum throughput a system can sustain; the phrases are meaningless because throughput is never measured properly
The ability to add machines; the phrases are meaningless because all systems can add machines
Linear growth in capacity with cost; the phrases are meaningless because cost curves are never linear

questions.explanation: And the related question: how can we add computing resources to handle the additional load?

questions.question: Why does the chapter insist on describing load before discussing growth?

options.text: Because load is easier to measure than growth
Because you cannot ask 'what happens if our load doubles?' until you have succinctly described the current load with load parameters
Because growth forecasts are always wrong
Because load determines the choice of database

questions.explanation: Load parameters come first; growth questions are meaningless without them.

questions.question: What determines the best choice of load parameters?

options.text: Industry benchmarks
It depends on the architecture of your system — perhaps the average case matters, or perhaps your bottleneck is dominated by a small number of extreme cases
Always requests per second
The database vendor's guidance

questions.explanation: Examples include requests per second to a web server, the ratio of reads to writes in a database, simultaneously active users in a chat room, and the hit rate on a cache.

questions.question: Twitter's November 2012 figures: post tweet and home timeline. Which pair is right, and where does the chapter say the difficulty lies?

options.text: Post tweet 300k/sec, home timeline 4.6k/sec; the difficulty is write volume
Post tweet 4.6k requests/sec average (over 12k/sec at peak), home timeline 300k requests/sec; the difficulty is not tweet volume but fan-out
Post tweet 12k/sec, home timeline 45k/sec; the difficulty is storage
Post tweet 4.6k/sec, home timeline 30M/sec; the difficulty is network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Handling 12,000 writes/sec would be fairly easy. Twitter's scaling challenge is fan-out: each user follows many people and is followed by many people.

questions.question: Where is the term 'fan-out' borrowed from, and what does it mean in transaction processing systems?

options.text: Fluid dynamics; the spread of load across shards
Electronic engineering; the number of requests to other services needed to serve one incoming request
Broadcast radio; the number of subscribers to a topic
Graph theory; the out-degree of a node

questions.explanation: In electronics it describes the number of logic gate inputs attached to one gate's output.

questions.question: Which metaphor does the chapter use for approach 2 to Twitter's timeline problem?

options.text: A ledger of tweets
A cache for each user's home timeline — like a mailbox of tweets for each recipient user
A firehose of tweets
A ring buffer of tweets

questions.explanation: Approach 1 inserts into a global collection of tweets and joins at read time (expensive reads); approach 2 computes the timeline ahead of time, at write time.

questions.question: Give the quantitative reason Twitter moved from approach 1 to approach 2.

options.text: The average rate of published tweets is almost two orders of magnitude lower than the rate of home timeline reads, so it is preferable to do more work at write time and less at read time
Reads were two orders of magnitude cheaper than writes
Storage costs fell by two orders of magnitude
SQL joins could not be indexed

questions.explanation: 4.6k writes/sec versus 300k reads/sec is roughly a 65x gap, which the chapter rounds to almost two orders of magnitude.

questions.question: A tweet is delivered to about 75 followers on average. What write load does approach 2 create, and what worst case does the chapter name?

options.text: About 345k writes/sec to home timeline caches; worst case, a user with over 30 million followers means over 30 million writes for a single tweet, and the chapter wants timelines delivered within five seconds
About 345k writes/sec; worst case 1 million writes, delivered within one minute
About 4.6k writes/sec; worst case 30 million writes within five minutes
About 12k writes/sec; worst case 300k writes within one second

questions.explanation: 4.6k tweets/sec times 75 followers is about 345k writes/sec. The celebrity worst case is what the chapter calls a significant challenge.

questions.question: For Twitter, what does the chapter identify as the key load parameter?

options.text: Tweets per second
The distribution of followers per user, maybe weighted by how often those users tweet
Total registered users
Read-to-write ratio

questions.explanation: The distribution matters, not the average — because it determines fan-out work. The weighting refinement makes it reflect actual write load.

questions.question: Describe the hybrid Twitter ended up with.

options.text: All timelines computed at read time, with an aggressive cache
Fan-out at write time for most users, but celebrities with very large numbers of followers are excepted from fan-out; their tweets are fetched separately and merged into the timeline at read time
Fan-out at write time for celebrities only
Sharding timelines by follower count

questions.explanation: This keeps the pathological case off the write path while preserving cheap reads for the common case — delivering consistently good performance.

questions.question: Once load is described, the chapter says you can investigate increased load in two ways. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Increase a load parameter and keep system resources unchanged, then ask how performance is affected
Ask how much you must increase resources to keep performance unchanged when a load parameter increases
Reduce the load parameter and measure the idle cost
Compare against a competitor's published benchmark

questions.explanation: Both questions require performance numbers, which is why the chapter turns next to throughput and response time.

questions.question: Which metric matters in a batch processing system such as Hadoop, and which in an online system?

options.text: Throughput for batch; response time for online
Response time for batch; throughput for online
Throughput for both
Availability for batch; latency for online

questions.explanation: Throughput is records processed per second, or total time to run a job on a dataset of a given size. Because of skew you have to wait for the slowest task to complete.

questions.question: Distinguish latency from response time as the chapter's sidebar does. Which one does the client see?

options.text: They are synonyms; the client sees both
Response time is what the client sees: service time plus network delays and queueing delays. Latency is the duration a request is waiting to be handled — latent, awaiting service
Latency is what the client sees; response time is measured server-side only
Response time is the p50; latency is the p99

questions.explanation: Conflating the two is one of the chapter's named precision traps.

questions.question: Which causes of response-time variation does the chapter give, even for identical repeated requests? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A context switch to a background process
Loss of a network packet and TCP retransmission, or a garbage collection pause
A page fault forcing a read from disk, or mechanical vibrations in the server rack
Variation in the CPU's clock speed rating

questions.explanation: Because of all this, response time must be thought of as a distribution of values, not a single number.

questions.question: What is the chapter's objection to reporting average response time?

options.text: It is expensive to compute
It is not a good metric for your typical response time, because it doesn't tell you how many users actually experienced that delay
It is affected by clock skew
It cannot be aggregated across machines

questions.explanation: The chapter also notes pedantically that 'average' does not refer to any particular formula, but colloquially means the arithmetic mean.

questions.question: A user's page load issues 4 backend requests. What is the probability that at least one of them is slower than the median?
questions.explanation: 1 minus 0.5 to the fourth power, which is 93.75%. The median refers to a single request, so a user who makes several requests is very likely to hit a slow one — which is why high percentiles matter.

questions.question: Your 95th percentile response time is 1.5 seconds. Exactly what does that mean?

options.text: The average request takes 1.5 seconds
95 out of 100 requests take less than 1.5 seconds, and 5 out of 100 take 1.5 seconds or more
95% of users experience 1.5 seconds
The slowest request took 1.5 seconds

questions.explanation: High percentiles (p95, p99, p999) are thresholds on the distribution's tail — they tell you how bad the outliers are.

questions.question: Amazon specifies internal service response times at the 99.9th percentile, affecting only 1 in 1,000 requests. What is the reasoning?

options.text: It is the cheapest percentile to measure
It is about who those requests belong to: the slowest requests are often those with the most data on their accounts, because they have made many purchases — the most valuable customers
It smooths out garbage collection pauses
Regulators require it

questions.explanation: Keeping response times fast for them directly affects users' experience of the service, and therefore revenue.

questions.question: Which figures does the chapter cite for the cost of slowness? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by 1%
A 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16%
A 10 ms increase doubles the bounce rate
A 5-second page load loses 90% of users

questions.explanation: Amazon's own observation, plus a reported figure on customer satisfaction.

questions.question: Amazon optimizes p999 but deemed p9999 not worth it. Which two reasons does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Response times at that percentile are easily affected by random events outside of your control
The benefits are diminishing
The monitoring tools cannot measure it
Customers never notice it

questions.explanation: Reducing response times at very high percentiles was judged too expensive and to not yield enough benefit.

questions.question: Define SLO and SLA per the chapter.

options.text: SLOs are the internal targets; SLAs are contracts defining the expected performance and availability of a service, which may allow customers to demand a refund if the SLA is not met
SLOs are contracts; SLAs are dashboards
SLOs measure uptime; SLAs measure latency
They are the same thing under two names

questions.explanation: Example clauses: a median response time under 200 ms and a p99 under 1 s, and the service considered up at least 99.9% of the time. The definition of 'up' matters, since if the response time is longer, it might as well be down.

questions.question: An SLA promises the service is up at least 99.9% of the time. How much downtime does that permit in a 30-day month?

options.text: 4.3 minutes
43.2 minutes
7.2 hours
8.6 minutes

questions.explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

questions.question: Why do queueing delays dominate high percentiles, and what practical consequence follows?

options.text: Because only a small number of slow requests is needed to hold up subsequent requests — head-of-line blocking — so you must measure response times on the client side
Because the network is the bottleneck, so you must measure on the server side
Because garbage collection is periodic, so you must average over long windows
Because disks are slow, so you must add caching

questions.explanation: A server can only process a small number of things in parallel, so even fast requests behind a slow one wait. Server-side measurement would miss that wait.

questions.question: When artificially generating load to test scalability, what must the client-side load generator do?

options.text: Throttle itself when responses slow down, to avoid overloading the system
Keep sending requests independently of the response time — otherwise it artificially keeps the queues shorter in the test than in reality, which skews the measurements
Send requests in a single thread for reproducibility
Match the production read-to-write ratio exactly

questions.explanation: A generator that waits for the previous response before sending the next one hides exactly the queueing effect you are trying to measure.

questions.question: You want percentiles on a monitoring dashboard. Which aggregation mistake does the chapter warn against, and what is the correct approach?

options.text: Averaging percentiles is mathematically meaningless; to aggregate response times across several machines you need to add the histograms
Summing percentiles; you should average them instead
Using a rolling window; you should use a fixed window
Reporting p999; you should report p99 instead

questions.explanation: The naive implementation keeps a list of response times in a rolling window and sorts it every minute; if that is too inefficient, use approximation algorithms such as forward decay, t-digest, or HdrHistogram.

questions.question: How often does the chapter say a fast-growing service must revisit its architecture?

options.text: Once a year
On every order of magnitude load increase — or perhaps even more often — because an architecture appropriate for one level of load is unlikely to cope with 10 times that load
Only when an SLA is breached
Never, if it was designed correctly

questions.explanation: Scalability is a moving target, not a property you design in once.

questions.question: Define scaling up and scaling out, and give the chapter's verdict on the dichotomy.

options.text: Scaling up is vertical scaling to a more powerful machine; scaling out is horizontal scaling, distributing load across many smaller machines, also called a shared-nothing architecture. Good architectures usually involve a pragmatic mixture of both
Scaling up means adding machines; scaling out means adding CPU. Scaling out always wins
Scaling up is for stateless services; scaling out is for stateful ones. Never mix them
Scaling up is elastic; scaling out is manual. Elastic always wins

questions.explanation: The chapter refuses the either/or framing: a few fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

questions.question: When is an elastic system useful, and what is the argument for manual scaling?

options.text: Elastic systems are useful if load is highly unpredictable; manually scaled systems are simpler and may have fewer operational surprises
Elastic systems are always preferable; manual scaling is legacy practice
Elastic systems suit predictable load; manual scaling suits spiky load
Elastic systems are cheaper; manual scaling is more reliable

questions.explanation: Elastic means automatically adding resources on detecting a load increase; the trade-off is operational predictability. Rebalancing partitions is where the chapter picks this up again.

questions.question: Why is distributing a stateless service easy while distributing a stateful data system is not, and what 'common wisdom' followed?

options.text: Taking stateful systems from a single node to distributed can introduce a lot of additional complexity, so the common wisdom was to keep your database on a single node (scale up) until scaling cost or high-availability requirements forced you to distribute it
Stateless services need consensus; the wisdom was to always shard early
Stateful systems cannot be replicated; the wisdom was to avoid databases
Stateless services are slower; the wisdom was to cache everything

questions.explanation: The chapter notes this wisdom is changing as distributed data system tools and abstractions improve.

questions.question: What is 'magic scaling sauce' and what is the chapter's claim about it?

options.text: A generic, one-size-fits-all scalable architecture — and there is no such thing, because the architecture of systems that operate at large scale is usually highly specific to the application
A proprietary Twitter technique for fan-out
A caching layer that makes any system scale
The combination of sharding and replication

questions.explanation: The problem may be the volume of reads, of writes, of data to store, the complexity of the data, the response time requirements, the access patterns, or some mixture — plus many more issues.

questions.question: Compare a system designed for 100,000 requests/sec of 1 kB each with one for 3 requests/min of 2 GB each. What does the chapter conclude?

options.text: Both have the same data throughput — about 100 MB/s — but the systems will look very different, so throughput alone does not determine architecture
The first has 100x the throughput, so it needs 100x the machines
The second is easier because it has fewer requests
Throughput is the only load parameter that matters

questions.explanation: 100,000 x 1 kB/s is 100 MB/s; 3 x 2 GB/min is 6 GB/min, also 100 MB/s. Identical on that metric, utterly different in design.

questions.question: An architecture that scales well is built around assumptions about which operations are common and which are rare. What does the chapter advise early-stage products?

options.text: If those assumptions are wrong the scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive; for early-stage products it is usually more important to be able to iterate quickly on product features than to scale to some hypothetical future load
Design for 1000x expected load from day one
Choose a NoSQL database to keep options open
Hire a dedicated scalability team before launch

questions.explanation: Even so, scalable architectures are built from general-purpose building blocks arranged in familiar patterns.

questions.question: What does the chapter claim about where the cost of software lives?

options.text: The majority of the cost of software is not in its initial development, but in its ongoing maintenance — fixing bugs, keeping systems operational, investigating failures, adapting to new platforms, modifying for new use cases, repaying technical debt, and adding new features
Most cost is in initial development, so ship fast and rewrite later
Most cost is in infrastructure, not people
Most cost is in testing

questions.explanation: This is why the chapter treats maintainability as a first-class concern rather than an afterthought.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say it is hard to give general recommendations for dealing with legacy systems?

options.text: Because every legacy system is unpleasant in its own way — so instead of general advice it concludes we should try to avoid creating legacy software ourselves, designing to minimize pain during maintenance
Because legacy systems are always undocumented
Because rewriting is always the answer
Because legacy systems are outside the book's scope

questions.explanation: The three design principles — operability, simplicity, evolvability — are the chapter's answer to 'how do I not create one of these?'

questions.question: The chapter defines simplicity as 'make it easy for new engineers to understand the system, by removing as much complexity as possible'. Which clarification does it attach?

options.text: That this is not the same as simplicity of the user interface
That simplicity requires reducing functionality
That simplicity must be traded off against reliability
That simplicity only applies to code, not to data models

questions.explanation: Internal simplicity for engineers, not surface simplicity for users. The chapter also notes evolvability goes by other names: extensibility, modifiability, or plasticity.

questions.question: Explain the quoted claim that 'good operations can often work around the limitations of bad (or incomplete) software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations', and the caveat about automation.

options.text: Operations is the load-bearing layer; and while some operational aspects can and should be automated, it is still up to humans to set up that automation in the first place and to make sure it's working correctly
Operations should be fully automated, removing humans entirely
Bad software cannot be rescued by any amount of operational skill
Automation makes operations teams unnecessary

questions.explanation: Automation does not remove the human, it relocates the human's job.

questions.question: Which responsibility of a good operations team does the chapter list that is about the organization rather than the machines?

options.text: Monitoring the health of the system and quickly restoring service
Preserving the organization's knowledge about the system, even as individual people come and go
Keeping software and platforms up to date, including security patches
Establishing good practices and tools for deployment and configuration management

questions.explanation: The list of ten includes tracking down causes, keeping platforms patched, watching how systems affect each other, anticipating problems, and defining processes that make operations predictable.

questions.question: Which ways can data systems make routine operational tasks easy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Providing visibility into runtime behaviour and internals, with good monitoring
Avoiding dependency on individual machines, so machines can be taken down while the system keeps running
Exhibiting predictable behaviour — if I do X, Y will happen — and providing good default behaviour while letting administrators override it
Hiding all configuration knobs, so operators cannot set anything incorrectly

questions.explanation: Also on the list: self-healing where appropriate, but giving administrators manual control over the system state. Note two deliberate pairs of opposites — good defaults plus freedom to override, and self-healing plus manual control. Removing control is not on the list.

questions.question: What is a 'big ball of mud', and which symptoms of complexity does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Explosion of the state space, and tight coupling of modules
Tangled dependencies, and inconsistent naming and terminology
Hacks aimed at solving performance problems, and special-casing to work around issues elsewhere
An excessive number of unit tests

questions.explanation: 'Big ball of mud' is the chapter's term for a project mired in complexity. Complexity also slows down everyone working on the system, further increasing cost of maintenance.

questions.question: Why does complexity increase the risk of bugs, not merely slow people down?

options.text: When the system is harder to understand and reason about, hidden assumptions, unintended consequences, and unexpected interactions are more easily overlooked
Because complex systems have more lines of code and bugs scale with lines
Because complex systems are harder to test automatically
Because complex systems attract less experienced engineers

questions.explanation: The mechanism is cognitive, not statistical — which is why simplicity is treated as a reliability measure.

questions.question: Give Moseley and Marks' definition of accidental complexity, and why the chapter stresses that simplifying does not necessarily mean reducing functionality.

options.text: Complexity is accidental if it is not inherent in the problem that the software solves (as seen by the users), but arises only from the implementation; removing it therefore costs no loss of features
Complexity is accidental if it was introduced by a bug
Complexity is accidental if it comes from third-party dependencies
Complexity is accidental if it appears only under load

questions.explanation: The distinction blocks the lazy objection that we must cut scope to simplify.

questions.question: Why is abstraction the best tool for removing accidental complexity, and what second-order benefit does the chapter identify?

options.text: A good abstraction hides a great deal of implementation detail behind a clean facade and can be reused across a wide range of different applications; reuse also leads to higher-quality software, as quality improvements in the abstracted component benefit all applications that use it
Abstraction reduces the number of lines of code, which reduces bugs proportionally
Abstraction makes systems faster by removing indirection
Abstraction allows fewer engineers to be hired

questions.explanation: The second-order benefit is the one people forget: fixes flow to every consumer of the abstraction.

questions.question: What does the chapter say SQL abstracts?

options.text: Machine code, CPU registers and syscalls
Complex on-disk and in-memory data structures, concurrent requests from other clients, and inconsistencies after crashes
Network protocols and serialization formats
Schema evolution and migrations

questions.explanation: High-level programming languages abstract machine code, CPU registers and syscalls. The chapter's point: we are still using machine code, we are just not using it directly, because the abstraction saves us from having to think about it.

questions.question: The chapter does not claim abstraction is a solved technique. What does it admit, specifically about distributed systems?

options.text: Finding good abstractions is very hard; in the field of distributed systems, though many good algorithms exist, it is much less clear how we should be packaging them into abstractions that keep complexity manageable
That distributed systems need no abstractions, only good algorithms
That abstraction always leaks and should be avoided
That SQL already solved the problem for distributed systems

questions.explanation: Good algorithms are not the bottleneck; packaging them is.

questions.question: Agile already offers TDD and refactoring. Why does the chapter introduce 'evolvability' as a separate word?

options.text: Because those techniques were mostly developed at a fairly small, local scale — a couple of source code files within the same application — and the chapter needs a word for agility at the level of a larger data system, consisting of several different applications or services with different characteristics
Because Agile does not apply to data systems at all
Because refactoring is only about code style
Because evolvability is a nonfunctional requirement and agility is functional

questions.explanation: Same idea, different altitude. The chapter also links evolvability closely to simplicity and its abstractions, since simple and easy-to-understand systems are usually easier to modify than complex ones.

questions.question: The chapter closes by splitting requirements into two kinds. Which of the following does it classify as nonfunctional? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Security and reliability
Compliance and scalability
Compatibility and maintainability
Storing, retrieving, searching and processing data

questions.explanation: Functional requirements are what the application should do — store, retrieve, search and process data. Everything else is nonfunctional. And the chapter warns there is unfortunately no easy fix for making applications reliable, scalable, or maintainable.

questions.question: In the Summary, how does the chapter classify the kinds of fault, and what sentence links scalability back to reliability?

options.text: Hardware, software and human faults; and 'in a scalable system, you can add processing capacity in order to remain reliable under high load'
Transient, permanent and Byzantine faults; and 'reliability is a prerequisite for scalability'
Network, disk and CPU faults; and 'scalability and reliability are independent concerns'
Detected and undetected faults; and 'high load always reduces reliability'

questions.explanation: Fault-tolerance techniques can hide certain types of faults from the end user. Maintainability is about making life better for the engineering and operations teams, including good visibility into the system's health.
